I won’t go so far as to say that I don’t understand the hype around this movie. While I don’t think his performance was worthy of a best actor nomination, Timothee Chalamet does give a compelling and fully immersed portrayal of the titular character. This movie takes big swings, and I admire that especially with the state of modern filmmaking being what it is. Other than that, I have very little positive to say about this movie other than, “I didn’t walk out.” My biggest gripe: every character in this movie lost my support emotionally. I’m not of the mindset that every movie needs a likable protagonist, but give me at least one character to identify with. The minor characters that do shine are given almost no space to do so. I actually really enjoyed Tyler the Creator in this movie. I’m excited to see what he does next. So tell me why his acting talent (a huge part of this movie’s marketing by the way) is restricted to what feels like almost no screen time. Instead, he and almost all the other interesting parts of the movie are bulldozed by the Chalamet Show. I’m also not a fan of Safdie’s “anything can happen at any time” writing style. There is merit to having unpredictability in a story like this, but “let’s take a 30 minute detour in this supposed sports movie to watch Penn Gillette get murdered over somebody’s lost dog” feels like taking that concept a little too far. I’ve heard supporters of this movie describe it as a fever dream. I feel like they’re forgetting how awful it feels to have a fever.

Marty Supreme (2025) (german/english) Marty Supreme ist ein Film, der sich von der allerersten Minute an anfühlt wie ein Tinnitus, nämlich einfach nur nervig Der Streifen spielt in den 1950er Jahren. Doch anstatt authentischer Atmosphäre dröhnen im Minutentakt Synthesizer Melodien oder Pop-Hits aus den 80ern durch die Boxen. Was soll das? Und dann Timothée Chalamet. Mein Gott. Man möchte ihm nach fünf Minuten ein Beruhigungsmittel und einen Kamillentee aufzwingen. Seine Darstellung besteht exklusiv aus Hyperaktivität, hysterischem Gebrüll und einem Blick, als hätte er sich vor jeder einzelnen Szene drei Liter Espresso direkt in die Halsschlagader injiziert. Zu 90 % ist es hektisches Herumgerenne, schrilles Gebrüll und maximaler Hysterie. Die Turnier-Szenen wirken im ersten Moment ganz schick, entpuppen sich aber schnell als reine CGI-Parade. Die Bälle fliegen mit einer Physik durchs Bild, die eher an ein kaputtes Retro-Videospiel erinnert als an echten Sport. Kein einziger Charakter besitzt Tiefe, Sympathie oder auch nur den Ansatz einer Persönlichkeit. Marty Supreme ist lauter, belangloser Schrott, der sich nach dem Abspann zum Glück von selbst aus dem Gedächtnis löscht. 2/5 oder auch 4/10 Punkten —————————————————————————— Marty Suprem e is a film that, from the very first minute, feels like tinnitus – in other words, just plain annoying. The film is set in the 1950s. But instead of an authentic atmosphere, synthesiser tunes or 80s pop hits blare out of the speakers every minute. What on earth is that about? And then there’s Timothée Chalamet. My God. After five minutes, you just want to force a tranquilliser and a cup of chamomile tea down his throat. His performance consists exclusively of hyperactivity, hysterical screaming and a look as though he’d injected three litres of espresso straight into his carotid artery before every single scene. Ninety per cent of it is frantic running about, shrill screaming and utter hysteria. The tournament scenes look quite stylish at first glance, but quickly turn out to be nothing more than a CGI spectacle. The balls fly across the screen with physics that are more reminiscent of a broken retro video game than of real sport. Not a single character possesses any depth, likeability or even the slightest hint of a personality. Marty Supreme is nothing but loud, meaningless rubbish which, thankfully, fades from memory of its own accord once the credits roll. 2/5 or 4/10 Points

Before anyone gets on me, stops reading, or decides they hate this take: I understand why so many people like this movie. I can see why it scores so high. For me, it wasn’t even a decent film and here’s why. The core problem is that Marty Supreme seems to want both things at once: a portrait of an arrogant, self-absorbed climber, and a hero you’re supposed to root for. That tension never really resolves, and a lot of the film’s weaker choices come from it. Most of the characters are flat enough that it’s hard to attach to them. The ones that stay interesting are Marty Mauser, Wally, and the dog Moses. Rachel is the clearest miss. The character could have worked, but Odessa A’zion’s performance rarely holds attention. Her only decent moment is the argument with Marty after they come back from looking for the dog. Kay Stone is the reverse: a thin character lifted by Gwyneth Paltrow. Even then, it’s frustrating how aware Kay is of Marty’s real intentions, yet she falls for him anyway including with the necklace she gives him, which then disappears because of what they do. Too often the film has better performances than character writing, or better ideas than performances. Several side plots also do little for the whole. Ezra Mishkin arrives like a random gangster fragment: a boss who wants his dog back, as if a John Wick got stuck in this one. That thread might have supported Marty if Ezra had simply stayed a rich old man attached to a shelter dog. The Auschwitz material is worse. It functions more like a bad joke than character development. It adds nothing to the plot, and using a story like that just to land a cheap beat feels unnecessary. If it had shaped someone in a real way, it could have earned its place. It doesn’t. What does work is Marty himself as a construction. The arrogant, ego-driven hustler chasing greatness is a strong idea, and Timothée Chalamet makes him watchable. The ambition is clear and often compelling. The problem is the film’s posture toward him. It keeps nudging you to root for Marty. Wanting the opposite waiting for consequences to finally catch him would have made his wins hit harder. The character is interesting; the film’s protection of him is not. The direction is similarly uneven. Some moments are sharp Marty running from the police has real energy, the movement and framing actually matching his panic and momentum. Then other stretches turn heavy without payoff, like the escape with Wally from the gas station, where the scene feels chaotic and overbearing rather than controlled. Marty Supreme has a creative premise and a few strong pieces, but more that doesn’t land than that does. I went in with high hopes and left disappointed. Tyler was good tho. Also, that sperm race: another weak joke in a movie that already has too many, and a pretty clear sign of a scene the film did not need.

Perché sarebbe stata un'ingiustizia verso le altre GIGANTI performance che non sono state prese in considerazione tanto quanto Marty Supreme. Non fraintendete, qui è incredibile, ma probabilmente non si avvicina alla sua top 3. Sono dell'opinione che la pubblicità ed il marketing, abbiano reso iconico questo film, perché altrimenti non se ne sarebbe parlato così tanto. Safdie fa un lavoro sublime, il personaggio di Marty è scritto e messo in scena in un modo quasi unico. Mi è pesato particolarmente stargli dietro, più volte ho provato fastidio nel sentirlo parlare o anche solo respirare guardando le espressioni. E' proprio quel tipo di persona che non dovrebbe nascere, nemmeno per sbaglio. Narcisista, manipolatore, adulatore, ladro, bugiardo, truffatore, egoista. A livello tecnico con Diamanti Grezzi, che trovo superiore a Marty Supreme, ha già fatto vedere di cosa è capace. Qui ha comunque tenuto l'asticella alta, nonostante non abbia apprezzato alcune cose. Secondo me ci sono delle "problematiche" che sotto certi aspetti lo rendono debole: - il personaggio di Marty sovrasta completamente ogni altro personaggio all'interno del film. Sicuramente è una cosa voluta, ne sono certo, ma rende la visione troppo piatta in alcuni momenti. L'unico personaggio, che ha probabilmente un pò di risalto, è Kletzki. Ma solamente perché Safdie gli dedica 5 minuti di screenplay e gli da un'identità ben definita; - qual è il topic principale di questo film? è un (non)biopic, è un film sullo sport, è un film drammatico, è un film sull'ossessione. E' tutto, ma non è niente. Non è carne né pesce. Quindi cos'è? L'ho trovato senza identità. Trovo davvero ironico che alla fine della visione, l'unica cosa che mi abbia davvero colpito, è l'unica cosa che mi portava a non vedere Marty Supreme, Chalamet. La cosa che mi ricorderà di questo film è la pallina da ping pong, brandizzata ovviamente, che mi è stata regalata da mio nipote. Lo guarderò di nuovo però, questo è certo.

Fast-paced. Dramatic. In 1952, Marty Mauser (Timothée Chalamet) may just be a talented shoe salesman, but he has his sights set on something greater: he’s determined to become the first American table tennis world champion, popularize the sport in the U.S., and get rich by selling special table tennis balls. If only it weren’t for the Japanese competition and his constant money troubles… The biggest highlight of “Marty Supreme” is undoubtedly Timothée Chalamet, who plays his character with such ecstasy that you almost start to worry about his health. Marty may be a narcissistic jerk, but he’s not without talent—in table tennis and in other areas as well. He slides from one disaster to the next, repeatedly wriggling his way out of trouble with questionable means, but somehow never quite gets his act together. The plot moves at an incredibly fast pace, with the camera and characters seemingly in constant motion. You might like that, but you don’t have to—after a while, I felt a headache coming on, and even the soundtrack—which I found disastrous and obtrusive—didn’t help. The biggest problem, however, is that the film is far too long; it also feels dramaturgically unbalanced—they should have cut at least half an hour. I don’t think “Marty Supreme” is bad, but unfortunately, I couldn’t see the cinematic masterpiece that many other esteemed film enthusiasts have seen in it.

In a word, exhausting. The Safdies are masters at the sweaty nervous energy of the economically depressed, the abrasive, and the fast talking con-men of the world.  In Uncut Gems the propulsive nature of the constant wheeling and dealing, the sense of impending doom, and Adam Sandler's charisma kept the stress from becoming overwhelming and the character one you love to hate.  Wishing for his success despite loathing his actions. In Marty Supreme, the movie is more or less split into two separate and distinct tracks. One a fairly typical, but brilliantly shot, short sports movie.  The other, a scrabbling descent into layers and layers of cons, dodges, grifts, and hustles weaving in and out of one another for nearly two hours.  All of it wonderfully acted, with cameos galore, but utterly draining and seemingly endless. I find myself at a strange impasse as a result.  There can be no doubt that is an incredible and effective movie.  But I don't think I could ever deal with seeing it again. Highly recommended, but be prepared for a marathon of awful people being awful to one another for the bulk of the experience.

Every single scene with Chalamet is so strong just because of the acting and it’s remarkable. Even though Chalamet killed it, that doesn’t mean anybody else deserves less credit. Odess a’Zion also did a phenomenal job. That one scene where she’s in Dion’s bedroom was incredible to watch. But enough about the acting, the story is also near perfect. It’s technically considered a sports film but to me it was more of a thriller. I was so on edge during each of the table tennis scenes, and I loved the final faceoff with Endo. It wrapped up the whole movie so perfectly. He didn’t get in the tournament, but he still got to achieve the feat of beating his rival head-to-head. I loved this movie and this is probably one of my favorite sports films ever.
